svg.title: What actually gets verified — three layers: the type system is mechanical and complete (if it type-checks, the pieces fit), Z3 contract verification is mechanical and bounded (prove or counterexample within a decidable fragment, the remainder runtime-checked), and human intent is expressive but unverified — a contract can be a perfectly verified implementation of the wrong specification.
svg.text: WHAT ACTUALLY GETS VERIFIED · THREE LAYERS
Each layer covers something different; only the first two are checked by a machine.

g.text: Typed De Bruijn references mean every reference resolves to a binding of the right type, every call matches its
signature, every match is exhaustive, generics monomorphise correctly.
If it type-checks, the pieces fit.
Mandatory requires/ensures/effects, translated into a decidable SMT fragment: linear arithmetic, booleans, array
lengths, ADT discrimination and fields, termination measures. Proved for all inputs — or a concrete counterexample.
What the fragment can't decide falls back to runtime contract checks: still executed, just not proven ahead of time.
Actual correctness properties, not just interface compatibility.
Nothing checks that ensures(@Int.result >= 0) is what you wanted — a contract can be a perfectly verified
implementation of the wrong specification. SKILL.md steers models toward reasonable contracts; "reasonable" has
no formal backing. This layer is deliberately the smallest possible auditable surface.

svg.text: Provably correct relative to stated requirements — and the human reviews contracts, not implementations.
